script.text: Paris, at the Opera. Paul Morphy takes White against two allies, Duke Karl and Count Isouard, playing jointly. They choose the Philidor Defense -- solid, but passive, meaning it gives Black little room. Thirty-three half-moves later, Morphy has won. A miniature.

Both sides push their king pawns two squares. Morphy develops a knight; Black answers with a modest pawn step, shutting his own bishop in. White strikes in the centre, Black pins the knight with a bishop, then trades it off -- giving up a developed piece. White stands slightly better.

Here is the turning point. Black pushes a pawn to b five, trying to shove White's bishop away. But that's time spent on the edge of the board while the king still sits in the centre, undefended. Tucking the king to d eight was the stubborn choice -- ugly, but it holds things together. After the pawn push, White is clearly better, and Morphy's lead in development becomes a genuine attack.

And then the queen goes to b eight -- offered up, free to be taken. It's check, so the knight must capture. That clears the square. The rook drops to d eight, and the king, hemmed in on its own back rank by its own pieces, has nowhere to go. Checkmate. Morphy wins.
A miniature -- a game finished in just a handful of moves. Morphy played at ninety-eight percent accuracy, his opponents eighty-eight. Develop early; in short games, the faster army wins.
